summary: Use a binary heap (priority queue) to repeatedly access the smallest/largest element in O(log n), ideal for top-K, merging, and greedy-by-priority problems.
lesson: A heap (priority queue) keeps its smallest (or largest) element accessible in O(1) while still supporting O(log n) insertion and removal -- it's the data structure for "give me the next-most-important item" without paying for a full sort. That makes it the natural fit whenever a problem asks for the top-K, K-th largest, or repeatedly needs the current minimum/maximum as new elements stream in over time. Merging K sorted lists is a heap problem in disguise: keep one candidate from each list in the heap and always pull the smallest. The key efficiency win over sorting is that a heap only pays O(log k) per operation for a heap of size k, rather than O(n log n) to sort everything up front.
recognize_when: Problem asks for the top-K, K-th largest/smallest, or K closest elements
You need to repeatedly extract the current min/max as elements are added over time (streaming median, scheduling)
A greedy algorithm needs to always process the next-smallest/largest available item (Dijkstra, task scheduling)
Full sort would be O(n log n) but you only need partial ordering or the extremes

complexity.notes: Each push/pop is O(log k) where k is the heap size; maintaining a heap of size k across n elements gives O(n log k) total, better than sorting (O(n log n)) when k << n.

gotchas: heapq is a min-heap only; for a max-heap, push negated values (or negate on push/pop) and remember to negate back
Keeping the heap size at k for 'k largest' means popping the smallest so far -- easy to invert the logic and get 'k smallest' by mistake
Pushing tuples for tie-breaking (e.g. (distance, node)) can crash on unorderable second elements; add a unique counter as a tiebreaker if needed
